Does Cheaper Housing Make Life More Expensive?

Yerevan asking rents and conditional commuting and winter utility costs

5 November 2026

  • Introduction
  • Reproducible analysis
  • Statistical interpretation
  • Conditional conclusions and recommendations
  • Limitations
  • Reproducibility and academic transparency
  • References

Introduction

A lower advertised rent may leave more money for other needs. A longer commute can consume some of that saving through transport spending and time. This study asks whether those extra costs outweigh the saving for comparable rental choices in Yerevan. The answer is allowed to be either yes or no.

We study advertisements from one agency, not actual signed leases or a random sample of households. The main comparison uses two-room apartments, 45–75 m², advertised as furnished. Room and area filters improve comparability; missing renovation and energy-efficiency information prevents a quality-adjusted claim.

For each named district we construct an example monthly budget from its sample-median asking rent, median round-trip road distance, and median route duration. These medians may describe different apartments. The result is a modeled district budget, not an observed household bill or the median of summed apartment-level costs. Kentron is the central-area comparator; its homes still have their own journeys to the common destination, Republic Square.

Research question and competing hypotheses

Does rent saved relative to Kentron exceed additional transport, selected utilities, and optionally valued commuting time? For each named comparison, define Delta as its modeled cost minus Kentron’s. Negative Delta means the comparison is cheaper under that scenario; positive Delta means it is dearer. The competing possibilities are Delta < 0, Delta = 0, and Delta > 0.

An inferential null would be H0: Delta = 0, versus H1: Delta is not zero, with alpha = 0.05 fixed before results. We do not run a population hypothesis test here. One agency’s convenience catalogue, uncertain dwelling independence, and constructed budgets do not justify the intended citywide p-values or confidence intervals. This is a descriptive and sensitivity study. A p-value, even if available, would not establish causation or prove a hypothesis.

Two outcomes and their limits

  • Direct selected cost: asking rent + modeled electricity, gas and water + modeled commuting spending, in AMD per household per 30-day month.
  • Generalized selected cost: direct selected cost + modeled commuting hours multiplied by an assumed AMD/hour value of time.

These are selected housing-and-commuting components, not a complete living-cost index. Food, internet, waste charges, building fees, moving costs, deposits, health costs and full car ownership are outside the measured model. Heating is included once through gas. Valued time is an opportunity-cost scenario, not an extra cash payment or a verified loss of earnings. A zero time value must give exactly the direct-cost outcome.

Sources and what they can establish

Evidence Coverage and use Important limitation
WSE.AM catalogue and public API Active catalogue retrieved 5 November 2026; asking prices, rooms, area, advertised furniture, district labels and approximate coordinates Single agency; availability and last price-update date unverified; no open redistribution license established
Yerevan transport Public fare table inspected in the rendered official page Fares do not provide observed trip times or household spending
Electric Networks of Armenia Standard household day/night tariffs by monthly consumption band Tariffs are observed; our consumption amounts are assumptions
PSRC gas decision and 2026 statement Standard gas rate and confirmation of unchanged resident payments from August 2026 Household consumption and heating efficiency are not observed
Veolia Djur Standard 2026 metered water/wastewater rate Assumed household use; excludes special eligibility
Armstat wages 2025 national gross monthly wage, used only as a time-value benchmark Lagged national gross mean, not a renter’s net wage
OSRM using OpenStreetMap Two-way car-network distance and free-flow model duration, queried 5 November 2026 Approximate origins, no live traffic and no transit itinerary

All sources were accessed on 5 November 2026. Raw factual extracts, hashes, retrieval metadata and route replies are retained separately from processed tables. Only analytical housing fields were extracted; contacts, images, owner names and full address numbers were excluded. Source robots explicitly permits the public API, but that is not an open-data license. Do not republish the catalogue as an openly licensed dataset. The frozen 1 November agency district index is retained as separate context and is not pooled into this later listing sample.

The geography is named agency-labeled Yerevan districts. Outside Kentron does not mean outside Yerevan. Abovyan and Masis are not compared: adequate matched town samples and journeys were not established. One Masis listing mislabeled as Kentron is excluded. District labels and origin coordinates are not ground-truthed administrative boundaries. No map is used to suggest precision we do not have.

Reproducible analysis

Run this file from the project root using the verified R launcher. It reads local snapshots and makes no network requests during rendering. It needs the existing ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, knitr, scales and jsonlite packages. No package is installed automatically. All substantive analysis chunks run; no result is supplied by invented example observations.

Chunk 1 — Prepare a clean and documented R session

Research objective: Make the analysis repeatable and identify the software actually used.

What this code does: Loads installed packages, sets readable plotting defaults, and records existing package-build warnings.

Code:

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE, scipen = 999)
packages <- c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "knitr", "scales", "jsonlite")
setup_warnings <- character()
for (package in packages) {
  withCallingHandlers(
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(package, character.only = TRUE)),
    warning = function(w) {
      if (grepl("was built under R version", conditionMessage(w))) {
        setup_warnings <<- c(setup_warnings, conditionMessage(w))
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }
    }
  )
}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 140,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
dir.create("outputs/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
set.seed(116)
money <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, big.mark = ",")
chunk_results <- list()
software <- data.frame(package = packages,
                       version = sapply(packages, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))
rownames(software) <- NULL
knitr::kable(software)
package version
ggplot2 4.0.3
dplyr 1.2.1
tidyr 1.3.2
knitr 1.52
scales 1.4.0
jsonlite 2.0.0 
chunk_results[["setup"]] <- paste("R", getRversion(), "loaded", length(packages),
                                 "packages; recorded", length(setup_warnings), "package-build warnings.")

Expected output: A package-version table and a recorded environment status, without installing anything.

Actual result: R 4.5.0 loaded 6 packages; recorded 6 package-build warnings.

Interpretation: The verified executable is R 4.5.0. Some existing packages were built under a newer patch release; their warnings are preserved in the final environment record. Successful execution of this report does not certify every possible package operation.

Connection to our hypothesis: This establishes a reproducible environment; it supplies no evidence about housing costs.

Chunk 2 — Read the frozen evidence

Research objective: Identify the observations and official facts available for this study.

What this code does: Reads the agency facts, two-direction route results, tariff extraction and Armstat wage series from relative paths.

Code:

raw <- read.csv("data/raw/housing_wse_catalogue_facts_2026-11-05.csv",
                fileEncoding = "UTF-8", check.names = FALSE)
routes <- read.csv("data/raw/routes_2026-11-05/routes.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
tariffs <- read.csv("data/raw/official/tariffs.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
wages <- read.csv("data/raw/official/wage.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
raw$listing_id <- as.character(raw$listing_id)
routes$listing_id <- as.character(routes$listing_id)
flag <- function(x) tolower(as.character(x)) %in% c("true", "1")

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw$listing_id), !anyDuplicated(routes$listing_id))
stopifnot(all(raw$price_original > 0), all(raw$area_m2 > 0))
stopifnot(all(raw$transaction_type == "rent"), all(raw$property_type == "apartment"))
evidence_counts <- data.frame(evidence = c("Retained rental facts", "Source-tagged Yerevan", "Routed origins"),
                              rows = c(nrow(raw), sum(raw$city_source == "Ереван"), nrow(routes)))
knitr::kable(evidence_counts)
evidence rows
Retained rental facts 949
Source-tagged Yerevan 933
Routed origins 277 
chunk_results[["load-evidence"]] <- sprintf("Read %s rental facts, including %s tagged Yerevan, and %s network origins.",
                                           nrow(raw), sum(raw$city_source == "Ереван"), nrow(routes))

Expected output: A small evidence-count table; invalid IDs or quantities stop execution.

Actual result: Read 949 rental facts, including 933 tagged Yerevan, and 277 network origins.

Interpretation: The raw facts include other room counts, currencies and locations so exclusions remain auditable. The source’s active status is catalogue status, not confirmation of immediate vacancy. Creation dates are not verified price-update dates.

Connection to our hypothesis: These are usable advertised market records, but their existence does not establish the research conclusion.

Chunk 3 — Select comparable advertised apartments

Research objective: Reduce obvious differences in rooms, area, currency, furnishing and geography before comparing prices.

What this code does: Applies predeclared screens, removes known ambiguous geography and one mixed-term offer, and conservatively screens possible duplicates.

Code:

yerevan <- raw %>% filter(city_source == "Ереван")
room_area <- yerevan %>% filter(rooms == 2, area_m2 >= 45, area_m2 <= 75)
candidates <- room_area %>%
  filter(currency_original == "AMD", !flag(is_duplicate_source),
         !flag(is_part_of_house_source))
furnished <- candidates %>% filter(flag(furniture_feature_present))
located <- furnished %>%
  filter(!flag(repeated_centre_coordinate_flag), !flag(outside_town_name_flag),
         !flag(arinj_border_name_flag), between(latitude, 40.05, 40.30),
         between(longitude, 44.35, 44.70))

long_term <- located %>% filter(listing_id != "11834")
selected <- long_term %>%
  arrange(desc(source_created_at), desc(listing_id)) %>%
  distinct(property_signature_sha256, .keep_all = TRUE)
sample_flow <- data.frame(
  stage = c("All retained rental facts", "Tagged Yerevan", "Two rooms and 45–75 m2", "Native AMD, whole unit",
            "Furniture advertised", "Geographic screen", "Mixed-term offer excluded", "Possible duplicate screen"),
  n = c(nrow(raw), nrow(yerevan), nrow(room_area), nrow(candidates),
        nrow(furnished), nrow(located), nrow(long_term), nrow(selected)))

chunk_results[["screen-listings"]] <- sprintf("The fixed screens retain %s advertised-furnished apartments from %s native-AMD candidates.",
                                            nrow(selected), nrow(candidates))

Expected output: A sequential sample-flow table with all denominators visible.

Actual result: The fixed screens retain 276 advertised-furnished apartments from 302 native-AMD candidates.

Interpretation: Absent furniture features mean unknown, not proven unfurnished. The signature screen removes a possible duplicate; distinct units can share building characteristics. Renovation remains unobserved, so the selected apartments are only partially comparable. Some ads have future or limited availability.

Connection to our hypothesis: This reduces several alternative explanations for rent differences, while leaving important quality and selection bias unresolved.

Chunk 4 — Check both directions of each journey

Research objective: Use network distances without silently replacing missing journeys with straight-line distance.

What this code does: Joins cached car-network outputs, checks both directions and snap distances, and fixes one primary analytical sample.

Code:

joined <- selected %>% left_join(routes, by = "listing_id")
joined <- joined %>% mutate(
  route_valid = !is.na(outbound_m) & !is.na(return_m) &
    !is.na(outbound_seconds) & !is.na(return_seconds) &
    outbound_m >= 0 & return_m >= 0 & outbound_seconds >= 0 & return_seconds >= 0 &
    outbound_snap_m <= 250 & return_snap_m <= 250)
analysis <- joined %>% filter(route_valid) %>%
  mutate(round_trip_km = (outbound_m + return_m) / 1000,
         round_trip_freeflow_minutes = (outbound_seconds + return_seconds) / 60)
route_audit <- joined %>% group_by(district_source) %>%
  summarise(selected = n(), excluded_route = sum(!route_valid | is.na(route_valid)), .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(analysis$listing_id), all(analysis$round_trip_km > 0))

district_names <- c("Кентрон" = "Kentron", "Арабкир" = "Arabkir", "Ачапняк" = "Ajapnyak",
  "Давташен" = "Davtashen", "Канакер-Зейтун" = "Kanaker-Zeytun", "Малатия-Себастия" = "Malatia-Sebastia",
  "Нор Норк" = "Nor Nork", "Норк-Мараш" = "Nork-Marash", "Шенгавит" = "Shengavit",
  "Эребуни" = "Erebuni", "Аван" = "Avan")
analysis$district <- unname(district_names[analysis$district_source])
stopifnot(!anyNA(analysis$district), "Kentron" %in% analysis$district)
write.csv(analysis, "data/processed/analysis_listings.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
exclusions <- raw %>% select(listing_id, district_source, rooms, area_m2, currency_original) %>%
  mutate(in_primary_sample = listing_id %in% analysis$listing_id)
write.csv(exclusions, "data/processed/sample_membership.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")

Interpretation: OSRM supplies a car-road model, not measured peak travel. Approximate listing points and agency district tags remain uncertain even after snapping. Public-transport times below are separate road-distance-based assumptions, not these car durations relabeled as transit.

Chunk 5 — Summarize rent and remaining comparability

Research objective: Describe how the selected advertisements differ across named districts.

What this code does: Calculates counts, rent spread, area spread and medians of already-summed round-trip road inputs.

Code:

districts <- analysis %>% group_by(district) %>% summarise(
  n = n(), rent = median(price_original), rent_q1 = quantile(price_original, 0.25),
  rent_q3 = quantile(price_original, 0.75), area = median(area_m2),
  area_q1 = quantile(area_m2, 0.25), area_q3 = quantile(area_m2, 0.75),
  round_trip_km = median(round_trip_km),
  freeflow_minutes = median(round_trip_freeflow_minutes),
  missing_building = sum(is.na(building_type_source) | building_type_source == ""), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(rent)
district_order <- districts$district
district_labels <- setNames(paste0(districts$district, " (n=", districts$n, ")"), districts$district)
summary_display <- districts %>% select(district, n, rent, rent_q1, rent_q3, area, area_q1, area_q3)

Research objective: See both the rent differences and the variation hidden by district medians.

  nrow(analysis), money(central_rent), money(min(districts$rent)))

Expected output: One distribution chart, not a predicted price pattern.

Actual result: The chart displays all 276 primary advertisements; Kentron’s median is 500,000 AMD and the lowest district median is 350,000 AMD.

Chunk 8 — Separate verified tariffs from assumed consumption

Research objective: Define an explicit winter-month household and time-value benchmark.

What this code does: Uses official tariff facts while keeping consumption, working hours and travel assumptions visible.

Code:

rates <- setNames(tariffs$value, tariffs$parameter)
wage_2025 <- wages$Value[wages$Year == 2025]
stopifnot(length(wage_2025) == 1)
paid_hours_assumed <- 22 * 8
hourly_benchmark <- wage_2025 / paid_hours_assumed
time_fractions <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1)
half_time_value <- 0.5 * hourly_benchmark
days <- 22
commuters <- 1
utility_parts <- data.frame(component = c("Electricity: 150 day + 50 night kWh", "Gas: 100 m3", "Water: 8 m3"),
  amd = c(150 * rates["electric_day_low"] + 50 * rates["electric_night_low"],
          100 * rates["gas_per_1000m3"] / 1000, 8 * rates["water_per_m3"]))
utilities <- sum(utility_parts$amd)

  money(utilities), money(wage_2025), hourly_benchmark, half_time_value)

Actual result: The modeled winter utilities total 24,769 AMD. Armstat’s 2025 gross wage is 303,140 AMD/month; the assumed hourly benchmark is 1722.39 AMD and its half-value is 861.19 AMD/hour.

Interpretation: Equal consumption makes baseline utility costs equal across districts. That is an assumption, not evidence that bills are geographically equal. The model excludes internet, building fees and other unsupported charges, and represents a winter month rather than an annual average.

Connection to our hypothesis: This prevents a hidden heating difference from being invented and lets the importance of time depend on explicit assumptions.

Chunk 9 — Define the financial calculations

Research objective: Translate the economic model into short reusable R functions.

What this code does: Defines five transparent calculations, using named units and special-case handling.

Code:

# Pure financial helpers. The Rmd embeds this exact code so it is self-contained.
# days = return-commute days in a 30-day month; commuters = household workers.
transit_cost <- function(days, commuters, boardings, fare, pass_price) {
  per_person <- pmin(2 * days * boardings * fare, pass_price)
  commuters * per_person
}

# The per-km amount is an assumed incremental operating rate, not ownership cost.
car_cost <- function(round_trip_km, days, commuters, per_km, parking) {
  commuters * (round_trip_km * days * per_km + ifelse(days > 0, parking, 0))
}

# Input minutes already contains BOTH directions; do not multiply by two again.
monthly_hours <- function(round_trip_minutes, days, commuters) {
  round_trip_minutes * days * commuters / 60
}

generalized_cost <- function(rent, utilities, transport, hours, time_value) {
  rent + utilities + transport + hours * time_value
}

# A positive threshold exists here only when the noncentral option is cheaper
# directly but consumes more commuting time. Other cases require separate labels.
break_even_value <- function(direct_difference, extra_hours) {
  ifelse(direct_difference < 0 & extra_hours > 0,
         -direct_difference / extra_hours, NA_real_)
}

chunk_results[["cost-functions"]] <- "Five small functions define the fare cap, marginal driving cost, monthly hours, generalized cost and positive break-even value."

Expected output: Function definitions; numerical behavior is checked later against hand-calculated cases.

Actual result: Five small functions define the fare cap, marginal driving cost, monthly hours, generalized cost and positive break-even value.

Interpretation: Private-car costs are a marginal operating scenario, not depreciation, financing, insurance or an observed fuel bill. Two-commuter car scenarios assume independent journeys/vehicles; shared-car savings are not modeled.

Connection to our hypothesis: These calculations operationalize both outcomes without double-counting transport or time.

Chunk 10 — Build consistent district budget examples

Research objective: Compare direct and generalized selected costs under identical household rules.

What this code does: Applies each mode to the district median inputs and compares every example with the same-mode Kentron example.

Code:

public <- districts %>% mutate(mode = "Public transport",
  transport = transit_cost(days, commuters, 1, rates["fare_single"], rates["fare_30day"]),
  round_trip_minutes = round_trip_km / 12 * 60 + 2 * 15)
car <- districts %>% mutate(mode = "Private car",
  transport = car_cost(round_trip_km, days, commuters, 60, 10000),
  round_trip_minutes = freeflow_minutes * 1.5 + 2 * 5)
budgets <- bind_rows(public, car) %>% mutate(
  hours = monthly_hours(round_trip_minutes, days, commuters),
  direct = rent + utilities + transport,
  generalized_half = generalized_cost(rent, utilities, transport, hours, half_time_value))

central <- budgets %>% filter(district == "Kentron") %>%
  select(mode, central_rent = rent, central_transport = transport,
         central_direct = direct, central_hours = hours, central_generalized = generalized_half)
comparisons <- budgets %>% left_join(central, by = "mode") %>% mutate(
  rent_saved = central_rent - rent,
  extra_transport = transport - central_transport,
  direct_difference = direct - central_direct,
  extra_hours = hours - central_hours,
  generalized_difference = generalized_half - central_generalized)

Research objective: Make clear how much of the rent saving is consumed by modeled extra transport and time.

Chunk 12 — Calculate conditional time-value thresholds

Research objective: Find where the district example stops being cheaper as commuting time becomes more valuable.

What this code does: Computes positive break-even values and plots cost differences across a continuous time-value range.

Code:

thresholds <- comparisons %>% filter(district != "Kentron") %>% mutate(
  value_of_time_threshold = break_even_value(direct_difference, extra_hours),
  threshold_status = case_when(
    direct_difference >= 0 & extra_hours >= 0 ~ "No saving at zero time value",
    direct_difference < 0 & extra_hours <= 0 ~ "Cheaper for all nonnegative time values",
    direct_difference >= 0 & extra_hours < 0 ~ "May become cheaper as time value rises",
    TRUE ~ "Positive break-even time value"))

                                  value_of_time_threshold, threshold_status), digits = 1)

Actual result: 20 examples have a positive time-value threshold; the smallest is 4555 AMD/hour. Other examples require their stated special-case interpretation.

Interpretation: Time value, not physical distance alone, determines these crossings. Car costs and journeys vary together, so a universal kilometre threshold is unsupported. A threshold outside the plotted range still exists algebraically when the table reports it.

Connection to our hypothesis: This identifies when the hidden-cost claim can become true under changed preferences rather than presuming one answer for every household.

Chunk 13 — Vary household, heating and travel assumptions

Research objective: Check whether the conclusion depends on a narrow choice of assumptions.

What this code does: Builds household/wage/heating scenarios and separately changes transit access, transfers and driving costs.

Code:

scenario_grid <- expand.grid(commuters = c(1, 2), days = c(16, 22, 26),
  fraction = time_fractions, extra_gas = c(0, 75, 150))
scenario_rows <- merge(budgets %>% select(district, mode, rent, round_trip_km, freeflow_minutes),
                       scenario_grid, by = NULL) %>% mutate(
  transport = ifelse(mode == "Public transport",
    transit_cost(days, commuters, 1, rates["fare_single"], rates["fare_30day"]),
    car_cost(round_trip_km, days, commuters, 60, 10000)),
  minutes = ifelse(mode == "Public transport", round_trip_km / 12 * 60 + 30, freeflow_minutes * 1.5 + 10),
  hours = monthly_hours(minutes, days, commuters),
  utility_scenario = utilities + ifelse(district == "Kentron", 0, extra_gas * rates["gas_per_1000m3"] / 1000),
  total = rent + utility_scenario + transport + hours * fraction * hourly_benchmark)
scenario_central <- scenario_rows %>% filter(district == "Kentron") %>%
  select(mode, commuters, days, fraction, extra_gas, reference_total = total)
scenario_rows <- scenario_rows %>% left_join(scenario_central,
  by = c("mode", "commuters", "days", "fraction", "extra_gas")) %>% mutate(delta = total - reference_total)

stress <- scenario_rows %>% filter(commuters == 2, days == 26, extra_gas == 150, district != "Kentron")
stress_plot <- ggplot(stress, aes(x = factor(fraction, levels = time_fractions),
  y = factor(district, levels = district_order), fill = delta)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(delta / 1000), color = delta < -90000), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "white"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~mode, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#246A82", mid = "#F5F4EF", high = "#B55B32", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-150000, 150000), breaks = c(-150000, 0, 150000),
                       labels = label_number(scale = 0.001, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "A two-commuter winter stress can change the answer",
       subtitle = "26 days; +150 m³ gas outside Kentron; cell values are AMD thousands",
       x = "Fraction of gross hourly wage benchmark", y = NULL, fill = "Difference") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

travel_grid <- data.frame(travel_case = c("Faster", "Baseline", "Slower"),
  public_speed = c(16, 12, 8), wait_per_leg = c(10, 15, 20),
  congestion = c(1, 1.5, 2), car_per_km = c(40, 60, 100))

                            travel_grid, by = NULL) %>% mutate(
  minutes = ifelse(mode == "Public transport", round_trip_km / public_speed * 60 + 2 * wait_per_leg,
                   freeflow_minutes * congestion + 10),

                    car_cost(round_trip_km, 22, 1, car_per_km, 10000)),
  total = rent + utilities + transport + monthly_hours(minutes, 22, 1) * half_time_value)
travel_central <- travel_sensitivity %>% filter(district == "Kentron") %>%
  select(mode, travel_case, central_total = total)
travel_sensitivity <- travel_sensitivity %>% left_join(travel_central, by = c("mode", "travel_case")) %>%
  mutate(delta = total - central_total)
transfer_test <- comparisons %>% filter(mode == "Public transport", district != "Kentron") %>%
  mutate(two_boarding_delta = direct_difference + transit_cost(22, 1, 2, rates["fare_single"], rates["fare_30day"]) -

commitment_pass_month <- rates["fare_365day"] / 12

chunk_results[["sensitivity"]] <- sprintf("Computed %s household/heating/time scenario rows and %s travel-sensitivity rows; %s noncentral grid rows are dearer than Kentron. This grid count is not a probability. Two boardings cost %s AMD per commuter under the 30-day rule; the annual pass amortizes to %s AMD/month but requires a different commitment.",
  nrow(scenario_rows), nrow(travel_sensitivity), dearer_grid, money(transit_cost(22, 1, 2, rates["fare_single"], rates["fare_30day"])), money(commitment_pass_month))

Expected output: A sensitivity heatmap and retained scenario/travel tables, without interpreting grid size as sample size.

Actual result: Computed 1584 household/heating/time scenario rows and 66 travel-sensitivity rows; 2 noncentral grid rows are dearer than Kentron. This grid count is not a probability. Two boardings cost 9,000 AMD per commuter under the 30-day rule; the annual pass amortizes to 7,500 AMD/month but requires a different commitment.

Interpretation: The grid exposes dependence on time, workers and heating. It does not assign probabilities to scenarios. Two-car cases assume separate commuting vehicles; shared rides could lower costs. Real traffic, timetables, taxi fares, social discounts and every possible household are not observed or exhaustively modeled.

Connection to our hypothesis: A finding that reverses in plausible scenarios supports a conditional recommendation; it cannot justify a universal claim about peripheral living.

Chunk 14 — Check aggregation and the narrower area band

Research objective: Assess whether a different summary construction changes the comparison.

What this code does: Calculates listing-level modeled totals as an alternative summary and reports rent-only summaries for a narrower area band.

Code:

individual_public <- analysis %>% mutate(mode = "Public transport",
  modeled_transport = transit_cost(22, 1, 1, rates["fare_single"], rates["fare_30day"]),
  modeled_minutes = round_trip_km / 12 * 60 + 30)
individual_car <- analysis %>% mutate(mode = "Private car",
  modeled_transport = car_cost(round_trip_km, 22, 1, 60, 10000),
  modeled_minutes = round_trip_freeflow_minutes * 1.5 + 10)
individual_totals <- bind_rows(individual_public, individual_car) %>% mutate(
  modeled_total = price_original + utilities + modeled_transport +
    monthly_hours(modeled_minutes, 22, 1) * half_time_value)
alternative <- individual_totals %>% group_by(district, mode) %>%
  summarise(median_listing_model_total = median(modeled_total), .groups = "drop")
alternative_central <- alternative %>% filter(district == "Kentron") %>%
  select(mode, alternative_central = median_listing_model_total)
aggregation_check <- alternative %>% left_join(alternative_central, by = "mode") %>%
  mutate(alternative_difference = median_listing_model_total - alternative_central) %>%
  left_join(comparisons %>% select(district, mode, generalized_difference), by = c("district", "mode")) %>%
  mutate(sign_changed = sign(alternative_difference) != sign(generalized_difference))

Statistical interpretation

No population p-values or confidence intervals are reported. The advertised properties were not randomly sampled from Yerevan’s rental stock, source IDs do not establish independent dwellings, and most cost inputs are modeled. Repeating a property across modes or time values creates scenarios, not additional data. The boxplot IQR is observed listing spread, not uncertainty about a population median. A bootstrap of this agency catalogue would not remove its selection bias.

If a representative, independently sampled dataset became available, the analysis would need an explicit estimand and sampling/clustering design before selecting a test. A p-value would measure incompatibility with that model’s null, not the probability that the hypothesis is true. A 95% confidence interval would describe a procedure’s long-run coverage under its assumptions, not a 95% chance that a fixed parameter lies in the computed interval. Statistical significance would not establish a practically important or causal effect. Here, model differences and sensitivity checks answer the defensible descriptive question.

Conditional conclusions and recommendations

The executed comparison at half the gross hourly benchmark is:

Private car: 10 of 10 non-Kentron district examples are cheaper than Kentron. Public transport: 10 of 10 non-Kentron district examples are cheaper than Kentron.

This applies to one commuter, 22 commuting days, the stated winter consumption and travel assumptions, and this agency’s selected advertisements. It does not mean that the same number of districts is cheaper for every renter or that any district is statistically proven cheaper. Direct and generalized costs must be read separately; the zero-time scenario remains the direct selected-cost outcome.

At the baseline settings, the lowest modeled generalized example is Erebuni for public transport and Erebuni for private car. These are conditional example rankings, not guaranteed available apartments or a citywide optimal-location recommendation. Sparse districts deserve particular caution.

The baseline model does not support the blanket claim that lower noncentral rents are necessarily erased by the selected extra costs. In the chosen household/heating/time grid, 2 noncentral rows reverse to a higher cost than Kentron. This count describes the chosen grid, not the likelihood that a household will face higher costs. The sensitivity figure shows the specified two-commuter winter stress comparison.

A household can use the comparison by obtaining an actual rent quote, checking the condition and heating system, timing its own outward and return commute, and replacing our assumptions with its own fare/pass choice, driving costs and time value. Lower rent is financially advantageous when it exceeds the extra cash costs; it remains advantageous in generalized terms only when it also compensates for the household’s value of additional time. The break-even table and sensitivity chart show where that conditional answer can reverse.

Limitations

  • One agency’s active catalogue is a convenience snapshot. It may overrepresent certain prices, districts, building types or clients. Asking rent is not agreed rent; creation date is not a known price-update date, and active ads can have future or restricted availability.
  • Furniture is advertised, renovation is unstandardized, and building details are incomplete. Area differences remain inside the size band. Neither narrow filtering nor the robustness checks makes this a causal or quality-adjusted estimate.
  • District tags and coordinates may be approximate. Known placeholders, explicit town mismatches and ambiguous border cases were removed; remaining points were not ground-truthed. Public road routes use OpenStreetMap contributors’ data, with cached OSRM model outputs, not live congestion or a transit timetable.
  • Winter consumption, access/waiting, congestion, marginal car costs and time values are assumptions. Full car ownership, shared-car commuting, actual taxi fares, summer/annual-average energy use and unsupported budget components are outside the model. Longer ticket commitments and eligible discounts can differ.
  • The 2025 national gross wage is a benchmark, not a 2026 personal net wage. Heating stress is not a measured geographic effect. No universal distance threshold, municipality-external comparison, or population significance claim is supported.
  • Changing the aggregation to medians of listing-level modeled totals changed 0 comparison signs; this is one limited robustness check, not complete immunity to bias or changed assumptions.

Reproducibility and academic transparency

The main source is this single Rmd. Supporting data, acquisition scripts, source metadata, frozen route replies, output tables and validation records remain in the project. A separate Word companion explains the same chunks and exact code. The report does not require a live website connection to re-run.

This work used Codex for source discovery, code, analysis explanations, and verification, with independent methodological and QA reviews. Sources and all numerical statements must be checked, and the student should independently understand and explain the work. The repository’s lecture examples do not establish the instructor’s AI policy or this project’s submission rubric; those remain to be confirmed before submission. The course’s familiar ggplot2/dplyr patterns guide the code; advanced methods were not added solely for appearance.
